items.title: 8 Most Suspenseful Thriller Movies of All Time, Ranked
items.summary: There’s no single definition of a great thriller . However, what most of them have in common is a sense of tension . Now, the way this tension is created can vary dramatically from film to film. Some thrillers build suspense through psychological mind games, while others rely on shocking twists that completely reframe the narrative in a single moment. A memorable thriller doesn’t just surprise the audience, though — it traps them, makes them question everything, and refuses to play by any rules.

items.title: 12 Sci-Fi Books You Need To Read, According To Blake Crouch
items.summary: Dark Matter author Blake Crouch has shared twelve sci-fi book titles that he recommends to his fans, and they’re a great place to start looking for your next read. Few modern sci-fi writers are as celebrated as Crouch, and a lot of that comes down to his impressive ability to blend science and existential fears in his books. Blake Crouch’s books make us think. They’re so influential that Hollywood has turned to them frequently as source material. In addition to Apple TV+’s positively-reviewed Dark Matter show , his writing was the foundation of Wayward Pines and Good Behavior . He’s also started screenwriting, broadening his reach.

items.title: The 5 Best Classic Books To Read in Your 30s
items.summary: Ah, your thirties, such a glorious, confusing time . You feel like you're too late to do so many things: buy a house, get married, have children, visit Thailand. Yet, you also feel so young — rather, you want to feel so young — and like it's still too soon to do a lot of things: buy a house, get married, have children, visit Thailand. items.title: Superman's Fascinating New Weakness Is His Best Since Kryptonite
items.summary: One of the biggest hurdles in creating a thrilling challenge for Superman to overcome is playing into his usual weaknesses, whether physiological or emotional. Kryptonite is a familiar solution, if extremely predictable, and magic is increasingly well-understood as something he can't reasonably resist. But adapting cleverly to his Kryptonian advantages is always a treat to see, especially when it's done by villains normally seen as trivial against one of DC's mightiest protectors. Batman/Superman: World's Finest plays into this nicely thanks to writer Mark Waid, illustrator Adrián Gutiérrez, and crucially for the colors in this instance, Luis Guerrero.

items.title: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review – Tarantino and Fincher join forces for Brad Pitt’s glorious return
items.summary:
David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s script, picking up from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and its lead is more ineffably beguiling than ever

We got through to the very end of Quentin Tarantino’s previous film Once Upon a Time in Hollywood without finding out exactly how, why or if Brad Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth murdered his wife. It was an issue only addressed in Tarantino’s novel based on the movie. And throughout the 140 minutes of this outrageous sugar-rush sequel – scripted by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher – this subject is tactfully passed over in silence, the one point that damages our perception of Cliff’s amiable-cowpoke good nature.

Cliff is the guy who climaxed the previous picture by helping with a dramatic rescue; after, that is, gallantly refusing an age-gap relationship with Margaret Qualley’s jailbait teen. Well, we may not get the complete picture of Cliff’s matrimonial circumstances until Tarantino’s forthcoming crossover Cliff Booth novel, with which this film is to form a kind of multimedia narrative event. But there is nonetheless such a huge amount of energy, fun, scabrous black comedy, provocative bad taste and film-making style to be had here.

Continue reading...

items.title: Alex Cox: ‘John Lydon said Sid and Nancy was a nightmarish piece of garbage’
items.summary:
The cult film director and Moviedrome presenter answers your questions on why James Bond is anti-Russian propaganda, whether Christopher Nolan is a bore and wanting to save Hunter S Thompson

Looking back, how do you regard your experience with Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas? And did you watch Terry Gilliam’s version? AwapBamBoogers
No, I didn’t watch it. I felt very sad about the whole thing because my wife and I were co-screenwriters. We went out to meet Hunter S Thompson and the poor guy was in a terrible state. He was hoovering up cocaine the whole time we were there. He had a great big TV screen, with a Post-it note saying: “Don’t watch too much TV.” We said we felt like his caseworkers, because all these guys in Hollywood like Johnny Depp were winding him up: “Dr Thompson, do something crazy, go out in the back garden and shoot a can of propane.” That’s all very well, but they were treating him like the freak in the county fairground. How many years was it after Fear and Loathing that the poor guy killed himself? He really needed an intervention. Instead, he was being encouraged by these Hollywood bastards.

The giant boar in Razorback gave me nightmares when I saw it on Moviedrome. Did it give you nightmares too? Sootsayer

On 8 December last year, the great director Rob Reiner signed off the prologue for Who Killed JFK?, his book written with David Hoffman and Dick Russell and based on his podcast with Soledad O’Brien. Describing a lifelong fascination with the assassination of John F Kennedy in Dallas on 22 November 1963, and what he saw as the vast conspiracy to cover up who really killed the 35th president, Reiner wrote: “Maybe, people don’t truly want an answer. Perhaps we are safer not knowing … Well, I’m done being safe.”

Six days later, Reiner and his wife, Michelle Reiner, were stabbed to death in their home. Charged with murder, their son Nick Reiner has pleaded not guilty.

items.title: You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable
items.summary:
Nathan Fielder’s intense close-range study of fraudster Elizabeth Holmes is as gripping as any thriller

• This review contains spoilers

Thrillingly reckless, deliciously irresponsible and as gripping as any thriller, this situationist docu-hybrid masterpiece from co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gets up close and personal with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes. It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger.

Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here.

items.title: ‘Sam-Bankman Fried messaged me from prison’: rising star Anthony Boyle on playing the disgraced tech bro – and a zero-hours bike courier
items.summary:
The actor’s latest roles see him go from a delivery guy on £40 a day to the notorious crypto scammer who stole more than $10bn. His sympathies are clear: ‘I wasn’t brought up to care about money,’ he says

In the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief Is the Thing with Feathers at St Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn. Afterwards, the 24-year-old actor hung around the stage door. “There were 500 people queueing up for Cillian, but I was the only one who wanted to meet Enda Walsh,” says Boyle, laughing. When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’”

Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. Then, a few years later, he received a letter from Walsh explaining that he was adapting Keiran Goddard’s 2024 novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, about five close friends from a council estate in Birmingham who find themselves questioning everything about their precarious lives as they hit 30. He had scripted the part of Patrick, a politically outspoken graduate working as a zero-hours…

items.title: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond | Peter Bradshaw
items.summary:
Pattinson is a character actor whose talent for inscrutable appraisal may mean a new era for 007. Will this more willowy, classy Bond leave sexism in the shadows?

• New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson
• Share your thoughts on the casting
• Pattinson’s journey from Harry Potter and Twilight to James Bond

If it wasn’t Bond … maybe it would have been Dr No in some hi-tech reboot. But Robert Pattinson – with his movie-star chops and track record in hip A24-type character turns, and his gift for cool, inscrutable appraisal and sensual menace – is an exquisite choice as 007, playing on the darker and more sophisticated notes of Pattinson’s performing personality.

And let’s hope, incidentally, that the actor now isn’t forced into a five-hour daily gym regimen to bulk up. I like the taller and more willowy Bond that Pattinson represents, the Bond from whose frame the tux hangs gracefully, the Bond with elegant abandon who’s a former British Naval officer, not a former US Navy Seal, the Bond who with a crinkly-eyed reptilian grin can style out waking up with a hangover after too many whisky-and-sodas at the baccarat table.
items.t: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond | Peter Bradshaw

items.title: The DCU’s James Gunn and Peter Safran are out – this is the biggest disaster to hit superhero movies in years
items.summary:
The adventurous weirdness of the Gunn/Safran era that fans responded to is now history. Can the DCU ever get back on track?

What was Warner Bros’ plan in 2022, when the studio decided to reboot its superhero output, jettison the increasingly muddled DC Extended Universe (DCEU) and replace it with a sparkling new DC Universe (DCU)? In part it was to wipe the slate clean after years of false starts, abandoned storylines and tonal lurches. There was a little bit of Marvel envy to proceedings, and quite possibly a desire to avoid having to ever again discuss Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice’s numerous failings. But mostly it was to take advantage of hiring of a man whom nobody could accuse of being short of ideas on how to make comic book movies. To a greater or lesser extent, the plan was James Gunn.

Fast forward four years, and that plan lies in tatters. Gunn and his fellow DC Studios CEO Peter Safran have this week been fired (though they will reportedly stay on as film-makers), and Jeremy Latcham, another former Marvel man, is the new boss. What is the plan now? Nobody seems to know, and there is not much point asking David Ellison, the man whose Skydance empire has now gobbled up two of the former big five Hollywood studios (Paramount last year and Warner…
items.t: The DCU’s James Gunn and Peter Safran are out – this is the biggest disaster to hit superhero movies in years
